title: Valentín Quiroz de la Sierra
text:
Dr. Valentín Quiroz de la Sierra (“Dr. Val”) is a Yo’eme social worker and data scientist from the California Yo’eme (Yaqui) Indian community. He is currently a Postdoctoral Fellow at the Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health. He holds a NIDA K99 Pathway to Independence Award (1K99DA066943) to support the IndigiText Project, a community-based participatory research project that partners with urban Native American youth to develop a culturally grounded text message intervention that uses reinforcement learning to personalize suicide and cannabis use prevention support.



Dr. Val helps bring the right support to Native American young people at the right time, using artificial intelligence built from the ground up with the communities it is meant to serve. His work starts from a commitment that Native American communities should decide what artificial intelligence tools are built to do, how their results are interpreted, and how they are used. His Indigenous Computational Approach brings Indigenous Research Methodologies into each stage of the artificial intelligence lifecycle.
This work centers on four areas:

Learning problem formulation: translating community priorities into domain knowledge that shapes model specifications and reward functions.
Representation and uncertainty: building compact participant representations and quantifying uncertainty in behavioral health prediction.
Sequential decision making: using prior evidence to support efficient policy learning from sparse or noisy participant data.
Simulation and evaluation: building simulation environments for behavioral health intervention design and delivery.




Dr. Val was a Point Foundation Scholar, a national LGBTQ+ scholarship, from 2013 to 2017 while attending the University of California, Davis. He graduated, with highest honors, earning a B.A. in Native American Studies. As a campus organizer, he helped coordinate the UC Davis Powwow, Native American Culture Days, and the opening of the Native American Academic Student Success Center. In 2019, he received The Brandon Harrison Award for Youth Leadership and Youth Organizing from The California Endowment for his community work.
He earned a Ph.D. in Social Welfare from the University of California, Berkeley School of Social Welfare, where he also earned a Master of Social Welfare degree. In addition to being honored as a University of California Chancellor’s Fellow, he was named a Human Rights Fellow by the Berkeley School of Law and a Computational Social Science Fellow by the Berkeley Institute for Data Science (5T32HD101364). He previously worked as a Child Therapist at the American Indian Child Resource Center in Oakland, California, and at the California Department of Social Services Office of Tribal Affairs and the Sacramento Native American Health Center.
In 2024, he joined the Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health. He also completed a fellowship through the Native Children’s Research Exchange (5R25DA061492) at the University of Colorado Centers for American Indian and Alaska Native Health. In 2026, he received the Advancing Indigenous Science & Engineering CLOUDS Fellowship at Adobe. He also serves on the US Department of Veterans Affairs and Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration Taskforce to Promote Suicide Prevention Among American Indian and Alaska Native Service Members, Veterans, and their Families.



IndigiText Project | IndigiText Project | Principal Investigator - A community-based participatory research project in collaboration with three Urban Indian Health Organizations in California, aimed at co-developing and evaluating a text message-based personalized just-in-time adaptive intervention (pJITAI) targeting co-occurring cannabis use and suicide risk among urban Native American youth. See In-Action ↗
HOPES Study | Helping Our People End Suicide Study | Principal Investigator - A community-based participatory research project in collaboration with the Sacramento Native American Health Center to develop a culture-based suicide risk assessment tool.
IWFP | Indigenous Wholistic Factors Project | Principal Investigator - A research project in which Native American youth helped choose and interpret the factors, utilizing the Indigenous Computational Approach to identify which combination of wholistic factors can predict suicidal ideation among Native American high schoolers in California. It identified ten of 17 factors linked to suicidal ideation, including depressive symptoms, school-based victimization, and sexual and gender minority status. Eating breakfast, one of those factors, was interpreted as a sign of physical and economic stability, not just a personal habit.
Native-RISE | Native-Risk Identification for Suicide and Enhanced Care | Postdoctoral Fellow - A randomized controlled trial evaluating artificial intelligence-enhanced suicide risk identification and care navigation strategies in three Native American-serving health care settings.
Cherokee Nation Storybook Project | ᏂᎦᏯᎢᏐ ᎦᏚᎩ ᏂᏨᏁᏍᏗ: Bringing Our Minds and Hearts Together to Promote Our Children’s Mental Health Through Storytelling | Postdoctoral Fellow - A community-based participatory research project in collaboration with Cherokee Nation Behavioral Health that developed Visiting Elisi, a storybook for a shared book reading preventive intervention. See In-Action ↗

title: Teaching
text:
My teaching philosophy is deeply committed to dismantling colonialism within educational settings. This mission extends beyond recognizing the impacts of colonialism on students’ learning; it involves actively challenging the pervasive processes of alienation that students often encounter in their educational journeys. In a variety of instructional settings, I incorporate the principles of Red Pedagogy to create more inclusive and equitable learning environments for all learners. Red Pedagogy is a critical pedagogical framework developed by Quechua scholar Sandy Grande that seeks to decolonize education by centering Indigenous knowledge and ways of knowing. This approach provides a pathway to confront the prevailing Western-centric educational paradigm, while also promoting social justice, anti-colonialist and anti-racist learning.
I have taught across diverse settings, from formal university classrooms and community workshops to online platforms. My teaching spans Social Work, Ethnic Studies, and Public Health. In community settings, I have facilitated health promotion education, cultural workshops, and teach-ins.
To learn more about my teaching approach, please review my essay titled “Towards a Red Pedagogy for Social Work Education” as part of the Teaching Effectiveness Award at https://gsi.berkeley.edu/sierra-2023/. [PDF]
